vignette:
He sits at his desk, the manuscript open before him, a red pen in his hand. The words blur—a love scene, two characters arguing in a kitchen. He blinks, sets the pen down, and rubs his eyes. The office is quiet, just the hum of the computer, but his chest is tight. He checks the door for the third time in ten minutes. No one is there. He knows this. He still looks.

He was born on a small island in the South Pacific, the eldest of five. His mother taught him to read beneath a corrugated roof, rain drumming above, her voice patient. He left at seventeen for a scholarship on the mainland, became an editor, married a woman with a quick laugh and a sharper tongue. For twenty years, he believed the bruises were accidents. She would apologize, cook his favorite fish, hold him at night. He believed her. He believed he deserved it.

The first time she hit him was in their third year. She was angry about a misplaced checkbook, and her palm cracked across his cheek. He stood still, stunned. She cried, said she was sorry. He forgave her. The next time, a fist to his ribs while he was bent over the stove. He told himself she was stressed, that he provoked her. He learned to walk lightly, to say nothing when her voice went thin, to make himself small. He edited stories of love and loss, of people forgiving each other, and he thought that was his story too.

The night he left, she threw a glass at his head. He dodged, but the shard caught his forearm. He looked at the blood, then at her face—twisted, familiar. He walked out. He was fifty-two.

Now he is seventy-four. Divorced twenty-two years. He lives alone in a one-bedroom apartment with a view of a parking lot. He does not date. He does not cook with glassware. His daughter calls twice a week; he keeps the calls short, afraid she will hear something in his voice. At work, he edits history books, preferring accounts of battles and treaties. He avoids romance manuscripts. His managing editor knows this, assigns him only nonfiction. The younger editors joke that he is old-fashioned. He lets them think it.

He sleeps in two-hour stretches. His dreams are not of his wife—they are of drowning, of being pinned underwater, a weight on his chest. He wakes gasping, sits up, checks the locks. The apartment is still. He does not call anyone. At the grocery store, he chooses aisles with wide space, keeps his back to the wall. A sudden touch on his shoulder from a neighbor makes him flinch, drop his basket. He apologizes, picks up the apples, his hands shaking. He walks home fast.

Once a week he visits the library, sits in a carrel, and reads old Pacific poetry—the words of his grandmother, chants about the sea and the sky. He does not tell anyone these poems make him cry. He wipes his eyes with a handkerchief, folds the book closed, and walks back through the rain to his silent apartment. He thinks about the woman who hurt him, wonders if she is dead. He hopes she is. He hates that he hopes that. The guilt sits in his stomach like a stone.

His work remains meticulous—every comma placed, every fact verified. It is the only thing he controls. When a junior editor asks his opinion on a paragraph about forgiveness, he shakes his head. “I don’t know anything about that,” he says, and turns back to his manuscript. He cups a warm mug of tea, checks the window. The parking lot is empty. The door is locked. He breathes.
